name: Jinja
comment: Hand-written for this extension; nothing vendored. Deliberately does NOT paint tags. A grammar hardcodes the delimiters, and a template's real delimiters can come from a `#jinja2:` header or from the `template:` task that renders it — so painting `{% %}` means confidently colouring literal output as a tag on exactly the files the server gets right. `textDocument/semanticTokens` paints tags instead, from the parser. Comments are the one exception and the reasoning is in `#comment`: they are painted here, and the server repaints the rare file where that is wrong.

interpolation-fallback.comment: The one shape worth keeping: `{{ … }}` with the default delimiters, painted only as a neutral punctuation scope so a template still reads as structured before the server answers. It names no keyword and no variable, so when the tokens arrive they refine rather than contradict, and on a file whose delimiters are overridden the worst case is a faint bracket rather than a word coloured as a tag.
interpolation-fallback.name: punctuation.definition.template-expression.jinja

comment.comment: `{# … #}` with the default delimiters. This one IS a guess — `comment_start_string` is overridable from a `#jinja2:` header and from the `template:` task, verified against ansible-core 2.21.3: with `comment_start_string:"<#"` the text `{# curly comment #}` is rendered verbatim into the output file. Taken anyway because the odds are measured: 0 of 1222 `.j2` files across seven public trees move any delimiter, and comment blocks are the largest runs of text in a template, so leaving them uncoloured until the server answers is the most visible gap there is. Unlike a tag rule this guess is recoverable — the server emits a `text` token over these ranges when the delimiters really were renamed, which repaints them to the default foreground. See `demo/templates/moved_comments.conf.j2`.
comment.name: comment.block.jinja
